entry.title: Quiz 2
entry.content:
You have 60 minutes (or until half of class finishes for a maximum 80 minutes) to respond to the questions and submit your answers.


  1. (score: 20) A satellite of mass $m$ travels in a circular orbit above the earth’s surface. What can we say about its speed (in terms of the known physical quantities)?

  2. (score: 20) A beach ball is dropped from rest at height $h$.
    Assume that the drag force from the air takes the form $F_d = -m\alpha v$.
    The governing equations for the velocity of the ball is the following:

    \(v(t) = -\frac{g}{\alpha}\left[1 - \exp(-\alpha t)\right] ~.\)

    Prove that the speed of the ball according to the above equation is sensible both immediately and long after the ball is dropped.
    What is the mathematical interpretation of immediately and long here?
    Hint: Recall the definition of the Taylor expansion:

    \(f(x\rightarrow a) = f(a)+{\frac {f'(a)}{1!}}(x-a)+{\frac {f''(a)}{2!}}(x-a)^{2}+\cdots =\sum _{n=0}^{\infty }{\frac {f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}}(x-a)^{n} ~.\)

  3. (score: 15) Show that the following holds,

    \(\large \nabla(\log(|{\bf r}|) = \frac{\bf r}{r^2} ~.\)

  4. a. (score: 10) A disk of mass $𝑀$ and radius $R$ is held up by a massless string, as shown in the figure.
    The surface of the disk is frictionless. What is the tension in the string? (score : 20)
    What is the normal force per unit length that the string applies to the disk? (score : 20)
    b. (score: 15) Let there now be friction between the disk and the string, with coefficient $\mu$.
    What is the smallest possible tension in the string at its lowest point? (score : 30)
  5. (score: 20) 2D Coordinate system rotation. Consider the 2D Cartesian coordinate system X-Y. The frame is rotated counterclockwise at an angle θ, as shown. Derive a matrix multiplication equation that can transform the position vector $(x,y)$ to position vector $(x’,y’)$.
    Recall that, \(\begin{eqnarray} \sin(\alpha\pm\beta) &=& \sin\alpha \cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha \sin\beta \\ \cos(\alpha\pm\beta) &=& \cos\alpha \cos\beta \mp \sin\alpha \sin\beta \end{eqnarray}\)
  6. Extra Credit. (score: 10) A ball is thrown at an angle $\theta$ up to the top of a cliff of height $L$, from a point a distance $L$ from the base, as shown in the figure. Assuming that one of the following quantities is the initial speed required to make the ball hit right at the edge of the cliff, which one is it?
    Justify your answer.

entry.title: Quiz 1
entry.content:
This quiz is open-lecture, however, you are not allowed to consult other resources or people.
You have 60 minutes to respond to the questions and submit your answers.


  1. (Score: 10) Show that the following identity follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem:

    \(\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1\)

  2. (Score: 20) Prove the following identity:

    \(\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin(\alpha) \cos(\beta) \pm \cos(\alpha) \sin(\beta)\)

  3. (Score: 20) Prove the following identities hold:
    a. (Score: 10 / 20) The double cross-product identity (also known as the bac-cab rule):

    \({\bf a} \times ({\bf b} \times {\bf c}) = {\bf b} ({\bf a} \cdot {\bf c}) - {\bf c} ({\bf a} \cdot {\bf b})\)

    b. (Score: 10 / 20) The alternate double cross-product identity:

    \(({\bf a} \times {\bf b}) \times {\bf c} = {\bf b} ({\bf a} \cdot {\bf c}) - {\bf a} ({\bf b} \cdot {\bf c})\)

  4. (Score: 10) How many scalar multiplications are generally involved in the multiplication of two square matrices of rank $n$?

  5. (Score: 20) Write down the set of equations that convert a Cylindrical coordinate triplet to a Spherical triplet.

  6. (Score: 20) Show that $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})^2 = a^2b^2 - (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})^2$.

entry.title: Announcement 1: Student-professor connection day
entry.content:
On the first day of our class, we will try to get to know each other. We will bring brownies to class and describe my research work and educational background for you and learn about all of you and your background and future goals. We will also review our expectations from this course. We will present the results of the survey that We sent out to you a week ago to assess your Data Science topical interests and knowledge, and your programming skills. Based on the survey results and your feedback in class, we will decide on the choice of language and the design of this course.

About Amir

I am a physicist and researcher, and currently a faculty member at the Department of Physics as well as the Data Science Program in The College of Science at The University of Texas at Arlington. You can find more information about me, our group, and our research at cdslab.org. Here is a summary of my life in a few pictures:

I was introduced to the world of information and computer programming around 1991 by my father and elder brother. By the end of elementary school, I was so impressed with and knew enough about computer software to write a few simple computer games in QBasic programming language on our first family personal computer, IBM 386. Here is an example of how computer games looked like 30 years ago.


I never imagined a day I would use computer programming for scientific purposes. Nevertheless, there has been almost no single day that I have not used scientific programming for my work and research, ever since I entered graduate school.

My research topics

The following are a few examples of what I do nowadays as part of my scientific research at UT Austin.

Theoretical Astrophysics

While my current focus of research is mathematical modelling of tumor growth and Monte Carlo samplers, I am and have been working in multiple branches of science and engineering for several years, from the subatomic world of elementary particles, to the microscopic world of biological macromolecules, to astrophysical phenomena occurring on the grandest scales of the observable Universe.

For several years of my research, I have been working on understanding Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) and their physics. Below is a movie of the moment a Short-duration GRB is generated from the merger of a binary Neutron star system.



Theoretical Biology, Bioinformatics

I have also worked for a few years in the field of bioinformatics and evolutionary biology. The overarching goal in the field of protein bioinformatics and biophysics is to understand how proteins fold into their unique structure, and what determines the stability of the protein 3D structure.






One of the workhorses of this field, is therefore molecular dynamic simulation to probe the dynamics of proteins and their interactions with other molecules. The following is a 1.5ns molecular dynamics simulation of Human Influenza H1 Hemagglutinin protein (1RD8, chains AB).


Petroleum Engineering


Computational Oncology

What you see in the figures below, is a representation of the growth of Glioblastoma tumor cells in a Rat’s brain over time.








The temporal evolution of the growth of Glioma tumor in rat






Monte Carlo Simulation and Integration Methods

One of the fields on which my research is currently focused, is developing Monte Carlo optimizer/sampler and integrator algorithms for Bayesian inverse problems.

Development of Monte Carlo sampling algorithms

Below you see example animations of two Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers, both of which sample a double Gaussian-peak function, but with different MCMC sampling parameters.



Development of Monte Carlo integration algorithms
